blocks.html: Database Consistency
blocks.text: Database Consistency

blocks.html: Data must follow rules defined in schema, constraints, and integrity checks.
blocks.text: Data must follow rules defined in schema, constraints, and integrity checks.

blocks.html: Focus: Validity of data inside one database instance.
blocks.text: Focus: Validity of data inside one database instance.

blocks.html: Examples:
blocks.text: Examples:

blocks.html:
If a table requires
age > 0
, inserting
age = -5
breaks consistency.
blocks.text: If a table requires age > 0, inserting age = -5 breaks consistency.

blocks.html:
If an order has
customer_id = 99
but no such customer exists → consistency violation.
blocks.text: If an order has customer_id = 99 but no such customer exists → consistency violation.

blocks.html: Database always enforces these rules, otherwise rejects data.

blocks.html: AConsistencyID (ACID)
blocks.text: AConsistencyID (ACID)

blocks.html: A transaction takes the database from one valid state to another valid state.
blocks.text: A transaction takes the database from one valid state to another valid state.

blocks.html: Focus: Business rules and integrity during transaction execution.
blocks.text: Focus: Business rules and integrity during transaction execution.

blocks.html: Example:
blocks.text: Example:

blocks.html: Bank with two accounts: A and B. Account A has ₹100 and Account B has ₹100.
blocks.text: Bank with two accounts: A and B. Account A has ₹100 and Account B has ₹100.

blocks.html: Data Integrity Check: Balance of an account cannot be negative.
blocks.text: Data Integrity Check: Balance of an account cannot be negative.

blocks.html: Business Rule: Total balance in the system remains same in the system.
blocks.text: Business Rule: Total balance in the system remains same in the system.

blocks.html: A transfer of ₹30 is recorded as deducted from A (A[100]→A[70]), but never added to B (due to some fault), the database consistency is maintained, but the total balance rule is violated, breaking the ACID Consistency.

blocks.html: Data Consistency
blocks.text: Data Consistency

blocks.html: Consistency as defined in the CAP theorem is often impractical and not required in many cases.
blocks.text: Consistency as defined in the CAP theorem is often impractical and not required in many cases.

blocks.html: To address this, other definitions of consistency have been introduced.
blocks.text: To address this, other definitions of consistency have been introduced.

blocks.html: These alternative consistency models are less strict than CAP’s consistency and allow certain relaxations.
blocks.text: These alternative consistency models are less strict than CAP’s consistency and allow certain relaxations.

blocks.html: All these forms of consistency—both strict and relaxed—fall under Data Consistency, but they are categorized with different names and implemented differently.
blocks.text: All these forms of consistency—both strict and relaxed—fall under Data Consistency, but they are categorized with different names and implemented differently.

blocks.html: Focus: Ensuring that clients see a consistent view of data, with strictness or relaxations applied as needed based on system requirements and feasibility.
blocks.text: Focus: Ensuring that clients see a consistent view of data, with strictness or relaxations applied as needed based on system requirements and feasibility.

blocks.html: Examples:
blocks.text: Examples:

blocks.html: Strong consistency: If user updates profile picture → everyone sees the new one immediately.
blocks.text: Strong consistency: If user updates profile picture → everyone sees the new one immediately.

blocks.html: Eventual consistency: If user updates profile picture → some people may see old one for a while, but eventually all will see the new one.
blocks.text: Eventual consistency: If user updates profile picture → some people may see old one for a while, but eventually all will see the new one.
